entry: Fictional island described in [[Plato]]’s dialogues *Timaeus* and *Critias*. Plato presents Atlantis as a naval empire from the west that had conquered most of Europe and Libya, an allegory on the hubris of nations. Set against the land-based [[Achaemenid Empire]] of the east, it loses divine favor after an ill-fated campaign against a fictionalized Athens and submerges into the [[Atlantic Ocean]]. The victorious Athens represents Plato’s ideal state from the *Republic*. Renaissance writers took up the allegory in works such as Francis Bacon’s *New Atlantis* and Thomas More’s *Utopia*. Nineteenth-century amateur scholars read the story as history, and its vague dating and location fed pseudoscientific speculation. The name became a byword for supposed lost civilizations. Scholars agree that Atlantis is fictional but debate its inspiration, which has been linked to the Thera eruption, the Sea Peoples invasion, the Trojan War and the failed Athenian invasion of Sicily.

Mountain range in the Maghreb, North Africa. The range runs through [[Morocco]], [[Algeria]] and [[Tunisia]], separating the [[Sahara]] from the [[Mediterranean Sea]] and the [[Atlantic Ocean]]. It is associated with the [[Atlas (mythology)|Titan Atlas]]. Its highest peak is Toubkal, in central Morocco, at 4,167 m. The mountains are primarily inhabited by Berber populations, and many of their plants and animals are endangered. The High Atlas was uplifted in the Paleogene and Neogene periods, when Europe and Africa collided at the southern end of the [[Iberian Peninsula]]. The range is rich in natural resources, including iron ore, lead, copper, silver, mercury, phosphate, marble and natural gas. Its subranges include the Anti-Atlas, High Atlas, Middle Atlas, Tell Atlas, Aurès Mountains and Saharan Atlas.

Philosophical novel by [[Ayn Rand]], published in 1957. Rand considered it her magnum opus in fiction, and it contains her most extensive statement of Objectivism, including reason, property rights, individualism and laissez-faire capitalism. It depicts what Rand saw as the evil of altruism and governmental coercion. Railroad executive Dagny Taggart and steel magnate Hank Rearden struggle against looters who want to exploit their productivity. The novel received largely negative reviews but has enjoyed enduring popularity and ongoing sales. It has been cited as an influence on libertarian and conservative thinkers.

Collection of maps, typically of Earth or of a continent or region of Earth. Atlases have traditionally been bound into book form, but many are now multimedia. Besides geographical features and political boundaries, they often include geopolitical, social, religious and economic statistics. The word came to mean a collection of maps from the mid-17th century, after the cartographer Gerardus Mercator published his 1595 work as a mark of respect for the Titan [[Atlas (mythology)|Atlas]], whom he considered the first great geographer. The first modern atlas is generally taken to be Abraham Ortelius’s *Theatrum Orbis Terrarum*, printed in 1570. Atlases also depict the celestial sphere, other planets and anatomy. National atlases began in the 19th century, and travel atlases are often spiral-bound.

[[Titans|Titan]] in Greek mythology, condemned to hold up the heavens. After the Titanomachy, Zeus condemned Atlas to stand at the western edge of the earth and bear the sky on his shoulders. He was said to be skilled in philosophy, mathematics and astronomy, and was credited with inventing the first celestial sphere. He fathered the Pleiades, the Hyades, the Hesperides and the nymph Calypso. In one myth, he briefly took the burden from [[Heracles]] to fetch golden apples. Later he became identified with the [[Atlas Mountains]] of North Africa.

Layer of gases that envelops an astronomical object, held in place by its gravity. An object acquires most of its atmosphere in its primordial epoch, through accretion or outgassing of volatiles. A body keeps an atmosphere longer when gravity is high and temperature low, and the stellar wind strips away the outer atmosphere. Aside from [[Mercury (planet)|Mercury]], all Solar System planets have substantial atmospheres, as do the dwarf planet [[Pluto]] and the moon [[Titan (moon)|Titan]]. The gas giants, including [[Jupiter]], retain massive atmospheres of mostly hydrogen and helium, while terrestrial planets such as [[Earth]] have heavier atmospheres of carbon, nitrogen and oxygen. Atmospheres have also been detected around exoplanets such as HD 209458 b and Kepler-7b.

Large-scale movement of air that, together with [[Ocean current|ocean circulation]], redistributes thermal energy across Earth’s surface. Driven by solar heating, the circulation carries energy absorbed near the tropics toward the poles. Its large-scale structure remains fairly constant, while smaller weather systems are chaotic and cannot be predicted in practice beyond about ten days. Each hemisphere has three cells: the [[Hadley cell]], the Ferrel cell and the polar cell. In the Hadley cell, moist air rises at the equator, moves poleward and descends near the 30th parallel. Surface air flowing back toward the equator forms the [[Trade winds]]. Over hundreds of millions of years, tectonic uplift can alter the [[Jet stream]].

Pressure exerted by the weight of Earth’s atmosphere, also called air pressure or barometric pressure. It decreases with altitude because less air lies above. A column of air with a cross-sectional area of 1 square centimeter weighs about 10.1 newtons from mean sea level to the top of the atmosphere, a pressure of 101 kPa. The standard atmosphere, 101.325 kPa, is roughly equal to mean sea-level pressure of 1,013.25 hPa. The highest sea-level pressure occurs in [[Siberia]], where the Siberian High often exceeds 1,050 hPa, with record highs close to 1,085 hPa. The lowest measurable sea-level pressure is found at the centers of [[Tropical cyclone|tropical cyclones]] and [[Tornado|tornadoes]], with a record low of 870 hPa. Pressure differences drive winds, and pressure is measured with a [[Barometer]].

Study of the Earth’s atmosphere and its physical processes, extended to the atmospheres of other planets. [[Meteorology]] includes atmospheric chemistry and physics, with a major focus on [[Weather forecasting|weather forecasting]]. [[Climatology]] studies average conditions and their variability over timescales longer than weather. Aeronomy examines the upper atmosphere, where dissociation and ionization are important. Instruments include satellites, radiosondes, weather balloons, radars and lasers. Atmospheric chemistry studies the composition of the atmosphere and its effects on living organisms, and has addressed problems such as acid rain, photochemical smog and global warming. Early pioneers included Léon Teisserenc de Bort and Richard Assmann.

Ring-shaped coral reef that encloses a lagoon. Atolls form in warm tropical or subtropical seas where corals can develop, and most are in the [[Pacific Ocean]]. In [[Charles Darwin|Darwin]]’s subsidence model, a coral fringing reef grows around a volcanic island. As the island sinks and erodes, the reef becomes a barrier reef and eventually a ring around a [[Lagoon|lagoon]], which is not the former volcanic crater. For the atoll to persist, coral growth must keep pace with rising sea level or sinking land. An alternative, the antecedent karst model, holds that rainfall dissolves a flat-topped reef into a saucer-shaped island with a raised rim, on which corals regrow. The word derives from the Dhivehi *atholhu*, a language spoken in the [[Maldives]].

headword: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
sort_key: atomic bombings of hiroshima and nagasaki
entry: Nuclear attacks on the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, August 6 and 9, 1945. The aerial bombings killed 150,000 to 246,000 people, most of them civilians, during the final days of [[World War II]]. They remain the only uses of [[Nuclear weapon|nuclear weapons]] in an armed conflict. The uranium gun-type bomb Little Boy was dropped on Hiroshima, and the plutonium implosion-type bomb Fat Man on Nagasaki, both produced by the [[Manhattan Project]]. The Japanese government ignored the Potsdam Declaration of July 26, 1945. Japan announced its surrender on August 15, six days after the bombing of Nagasaki and the Soviet Union’s declaration of war. Supporters argue that the bombings ended the war with fewer casualties and helped create the Long Peace. Critics argue that the bombings were unnecessary for the war’s end and were a [[War crime|war crime]].

Clock that measures time by monitoring the resonant frequency of atoms. The SI second is defined by the fixed frequency of the hyperfine transition of the [[Caesium|cesium]]-133 atom, 9,192,631,770 hertz. An ensemble of atomic clocks worldwide maintains the time scale on which [[Coordinated Universal Time]] (UTC), the basis of civil time, is built. UTC uses leap seconds to keep clock time within one second of [[Earth's rotation]]. Atomic clocks also support satellite navigation, including the [[Global Positioning System]], since a timing error of 1 nanosecond corresponds to a positional error of roughly 30 cm. The main type in use employs cesium atoms cooled near absolute zero. In 2025, the National Institute of Standards and Technology reported an optical clock based on a trapped aluminum ion with a systematic uncertainty of around 19 decimal places.

Mass of a single atom, derived mainly from the protons and neutrons in its nucleus. Atomic mass is often measured in [[Dalton (unit)|daltons]] (Da), also called unified atomic mass units (u). One dalton is one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom, so the atomic mass of a nuclide in daltons is close to its mass number. An atom’s mass is slightly less than the sum of its protons, neutrons and electrons, owing to mass defect, which is explained by [[Mass–energy equivalence|mass–energy equivalence]] (E = mc²). Relative isotopic mass is the dimensionless ratio of an isotope’s mass to one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom. Because natural substances are usually mixtures of isotopes, the elemental atomic weight is the average of isotope masses weighted by abundance.

Small, dense core of an atom, made of protons and neutrons. [[Ernest Rutherford]] discovered the nucleus in 1911 at the University of Manchester, based on the 1909 Geiger–Marsden gold foil experiment, in which many [[Alpha particle|alpha particles]] were deflected at large angles. The finding showed that an atom’s positive charge and mass are concentrated in a dense center. After the discovery of the neutron in 1932, Dmitri Ivanenko and [[Werner Heisenberg]] developed models of a nucleus of protons and neutrons. Almost all of an atom’s mass lies in its nucleus, which is held together by the nuclear force. Nuclear diameters range from about 1.70 fm for hydrogen to about 11.7 fm for uranium, roughly 27,000 to 60,000 times smaller than the atom. The branch of physics that studies it is [[Nuclear physics|nuclear physics]].

Number of protons in an atom’s nucleus, which uniquely identifies a chemical element. Its symbol Z comes from the German word *Zahl*, meaning number. In an uncharged atom it also equals the number of electrons, and for an atom with protons and neutrons, adding the neutron number gives the mass number. The natural elements run from 1 for [[Hydrogen]] to 92 for [[Uranium]]. Atoms with the same atomic number but different neutron numbers are [[Isotope|isotopes]]. In 1913 Antonius van den Broek proposed that nuclear charge equals an element’s position in the [[Periodic table]], and [[Ernest Rutherford]] used the term for that position. Henry Moseley’s X-ray spectroscopy in 1913–1914 showed that atomic number, rather than atomic weight, defines an element’s identity.

Function describing the location and wave-like behavior of an electron in an atom. It can be used to calculate the probability of finding the electron in a region around the nucleus. Each orbital is characterized by three [[Quantum mechanics|quantum]] numbers, n, ℓ and mℓ, which give an electron’s energy, its orbital angular momentum and the projection of that momentum on an axis. An orbital holds at most two electrons, with opposite [[Spin (physics)|spins]]. The names s, p, d and f refer to angular momentum values of 0, 1, 2 and 3, and they describe [[Electron configuration|electron configurations]]. Electrons exist as standing waves rather than orbiting like planets. The periodic table’s blocks of 2, 6, 10 and 14 elements arise from the number of electrons that fill complete s, p, d and f orbitals.

Field of physics that studies atoms as systems of electrons and an atomic nucleus. It is primarily concerned with how electrons are arranged around the nucleus and how those arrangements change, including in ions. Unlike [[Nuclear physics|nuclear physics]], which studies nuclear reactions, it considers atoms in isolation, focusing on ionization and excitation by photons or collisions. Electrons absorb energy from light, magnetic fields or colliding particles, and an excited electron that drops to a lower state emits a [[Photon|photon]] of the energy difference. Because atomic and nuclear are synonymous in everyday English, the term is often associated with nuclear power and nuclear weapons. Atomic physics provides the underlying theory for [[Plasma (physics)|plasma]] physics and atmospheric physics.

Chronic inflammatory skin condition, also called atopic eczema. It causes itchy, red, cracked skin and affects about 20% of people at some point in their lives, usually beginning in childhood. Scratching raises the risk of skin infections, and many people develop [[Asthma|asthma]] or hay fever. The cause is unknown but is believed to involve [[Genetics|genetics]] and immune system dysfunction. Treatment relies on moisturizers, corticosteroid creams to control flare-ups and avoidance of triggers.

Statin medication sold under the brand name Lipitor. It is taken by mouth to prevent [[Cardiovascular disease|cardiovascular disease]] in people at high risk and to treat abnormal lipid levels. Like all statins, it inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, an [[Enzyme|enzyme]] in the liver that is involved in producing [[Cholesterol|cholesterol]]. Common side effects include diarrhea and muscle pain; rare but serious ones include rhabdomyolysis. It was patented in 1986 and approved in the United States in 1996. It is the most commonly prescribed medication in the United States, with more than 115 million prescriptions.

Abnormal heart rhythm characterized by rapid and irregular beating of the atria. Episodes may be asymptomatic or may cause palpitations, fainting or shortness of breath. It is associated with an increased risk of [[Heart failure]], [[Dementia]] and [[Stroke]]. High blood pressure and valvular heart disease are the most common modifiable risk factors. Anticoagulants such as warfarin reduce stroke risk but increase major bleeding. As of 2020 it affected more than 33 million people worldwide.

Toxic perennial herb of the [[Solanaceae|nightshade family]], also called deadly nightshade. Native to Europe and Western Asia, including Turkey, it is also naturalized in parts of Canada, North Africa and the United States. Its foliage and berries contain tropane [[Alkaloid|alkaloids]], including atropine, scopolamine and hyoscyamine, which cause delirium and hallucinations. These compounds are also used as pharmaceutical anticholinergics. The antidote for poisoning is physostigmine or pilocarpine. [[Carl Linnaeus]] chose the genus name *Atropa* because of the poisonous properties of these plants.

Ancient Iranian kingdom (c. 323 BC–226 AD) centered on the present-day Azerbaijan region of northwestern [[Iran]]. It was established by the Persian satrap Atropates, and his descendants ruled it until the early 1st century AD, when the Parthian Arsacid dynasty supplanted them. Its name is the direct ancestor of the name of the historic Azerbaijan region. The kingdom was briefly ruled by [[Alexander the Great]] and later submitted to the [[Seleucid Empire]] while keeping internal independence. It was conquered by the Sasanians in 226 and became a province governed by a marzban. Atropatene was the only Iranian region to remain under Zoroastrian authority from the [[Achaemenid Empire]] to the Arab conquest without interruption.

Tactical military aircraft designed for airstrikes with greater precision than [[Bomber|bombers]], able to press attacks against strong low-level air defenses. It is built mainly for close air support and naval air-to-surface missions. Designs for non-naval roles are called ground-attack aircraft. [[Fighter aircraft]] often perform the attack role, and fighter-bomber conversions are counted in the class. A dedicated attack category existed mainly during and after [[World War II]], when aircraft such as the German Henschel Hs 129 and the Soviet Ilyushin Il-2 were built for it. Since the 1960s, only two dedicated designs have been widely introduced: the American [[Fairchild Republic A-10 Thunderbolt II|A-10 Thunderbolt II]] and the Sukhoi Su-25. Precision-guided munitions allowed almost any aircraft, and [[Helicopter|attack helicopters]], to take over many of these roles.

Surprise attack by the [[Empire of Japan]] on the United States Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on December 7, 1941. The raid was launched from six aircraft carriers in two waves of 353 aircraft. [[Isoroku Yamamoto]] planned it as a pre-emptive strike to keep the Pacific Fleet from interfering with Japan’s planned actions in Southeast Asia. Of the eight US battleships present, all were damaged and four were sunk. The attack killed 2,403 Americans and wounded 1,178. Japanese losses totaled 29 aircraft and five midget submarines. The United States declared war on Japan the next day, and on December 11 Germany and Italy declared war on the United States. [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]] labeled the date "a date which will live in infamy".

Japanese [[Manga|manga]] series written and illustrated by Hajime Isayama. Set in a world where humanity lives behind three walls that protect it from man-eating giants called Titans, it follows Eren Yeager, who vows to exterminate the Titans after they destroy his hometown. Serialized in Kodansha’s *Bessatsu Shōnen Magazine* from September 2009 to April 2021, it was collected in 34 volumes. An [[Anime|anime]] adaptation was produced by Wit Studio and MAPPA. By November 2023 the manga had over 140 million copies in circulation.
